meta.title: Research studio R2: finding out what is already known (the studio's own text)
meta.note: The one-line summaries are the course's own words, written from each paper's abstract on 3 November 2026 (first-pass coding); no abstract is quoted. Paper metadata and counts are in r02-literature-openalex.json (OpenAlex snapshot of the same date). The three-pass worked example reads the open preprint of Hilbers, Brayshaw and Gandy (arXiv 2210.08351, October 2022); check the published version for changes.

question: How do [[capacity-expansion|capacity-expansion]] models stand in for a whole year with a few [[representative-period|representative periods]], and what happens to storage and to [[extreme-period|extreme periods]] when they do?
coding_rule: Tick a cell only when the abstract says so. “not stated” means the abstract does not say: it is not the same as no, and a second pass can change it.

values.not stated: the abstract does not say (not the same as no)

ladder_q.q: Two changes at once: quote “representative days” as one phrase, and drop the model words. More results, or fewer?
ladder_q.why: Two changes that pull opposite ways: quotes narrow, dropping two words widens. The count rose, but this pair cannot show what quoting alone does.

ladder_q.q: Join three synonyms with OR. More, or fewer?
ladder_q.why: OR widens: a work needs any one of the four phrases.

ladder_q.q: AND the model block. More, or fewer?
ladder_q.why: AND narrows: a work now needs one phrase from each block.

ladder_q.q: AND the word storage. More, or fewer?
ladder_q.why: Another AND narrows again, and it can drop relevant papers whose abstracts use other words.

ladder_labels.phrase: Quote one phrase, drop the model words (two changes)

matrix.name: Poncelet et al. (2016)
matrix.summary: Picks representative days with an optimization and compares it with [[clustering|clustering]] and simple rules, using new measures of how representative a set is.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme days.
why.full: The abstract reports comparisons between selection methods, not with a full-year model run.

matrix.name: Kotzur et al. (2017)
matrix.summary: Compares [[time-series-aggregation|aggregation methods]] across several energy-system designs; the system matters more than the method, and typical periods as usually modelled cannot carry seasonal storage.

why.storage: The abstract names the seasonal-storage problem but reports no link between periods. Mentioning storage is not the same as modelling it.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme periods; only a second pass can say whether the paper uses them.
why.full: It speaks of the real system cost, but the abstract does not say how that cost was found: a second pass would tell.

matrix.name: Pfenninger (2017)
matrix.summary: Compares downsampling, clustering and simple rules in a Great Britain power model with 25 years of wind and solar data; the best method depends on the data and the model.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme periods.
why.full: It compares results across methods; the abstract does not name a full-resolution benchmark.

matrix.name: Kotzur et al. (2018)
matrix.summary: Links typical periods through a storage level that carries energy from one period to the next, so seasonal storage can be modeled, and compares with optimizing the full year.

why.storage: The abstract gives this as its contribution: a storage state that connects the periods in sequence.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme periods.
why.full: The abstract reports a comparison with models of the full annual series.

matrix.name: Liu, Sioshansi and Conejo (2017)
matrix.summary: Picks representative days with two hierarchical clustering methods that keep correlations in time and between places, tested on the Texas power system against the full data.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme days.
why.full: The abstract reports investment decisions compared with those from the full, unclustered data.

matrix.name: Tejada-Arango et al. (2018)
matrix.summary: Adds links between representative days so that long-term storage fits an investment model, and benchmarks it against an hourly [[unit-commitment|unit-commitment]] model.

why.storage: The abstract reports a transition matrix between representative days that carries long-term storage.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme days.
why.full: The abstract names an hourly [[unit-commitment|unit-commitment]] model as the benchmark.

matrix.name: Mallapragada et al. (2018)
matrix.summary: Compares a model with up to 12 representative days against a time-slice model for Texas, then runs both plans through an hourly operations model.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme days.
why.full: The abstract reports both plans tested in an hourly grid-operations model.

matrix.name: Teichgraeber and Brandt (2019)
matrix.summary: Compares five clustering methods on two operating problems, battery and gas-turbine scheduling; a better clustering score does not always give a better result.

why.storage: The abstract names battery scheduling but reports no link between periods.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme periods.
why.full: It compares objective values; the abstract does not say against what.

matrix.name: Sun et al. (2019)
matrix.summary: Groups days by the investment decisions each day would lead to, rather than by the input data alone, for large power systems with many locations.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme days.
why.full: The abstract names no full-year benchmark.

matrix.name: Yeganefar et al. (2020)
matrix.summary: Adds extreme days of high and low [[net-demand|net load]] to the representative days, picked with [[self-organizing-map|self-organizing maps]], and tests them on two power systems.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.extreme: The abstract gives extreme days of [[net-demand|net load]] as its contribution.
why.full: It reports better operating-cost estimates; the abstract does not say against what.

matrix.name: Teichgraeber, Küpper and Brandt (2021)
matrix.summary: Adds extreme periods one at a time, using the planning model's own results, until the design meets demand in every hour of the full data.

why.storage: The abstract does not say whether storage links the periods; a second pass would check.
why.extreme: The abstract gives extreme periods, found from the model's results, as its contribution.
why.full: The abstract reports the design checked on the full input data.

matrix.name: Reichenberg and Hedenus (2022)
matrix.summary: Measures how representative periods distort cost and capacity results against a full chronological year, in a European model where wind and solar supply 90% of generation.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.extreme: The abstract does not mention extreme periods.
why.full: The abstract names a full chronological year as the benchmark.

fillers.name: Hilbers, Brayshaw and Gandy (2023)
fillers.summary: Picks periods after a first model run, keeps the extreme periods that drive capacity, and keeps chronology so storage can be modelled.

fillers.name: Moradi-Sepahvand and Tindemans (2023)
fillers.summary: A clustering-based aggregation that keeps extreme values and the order of days, for planning lines with short- and long-term storage on a six-bus test system.

fillers.name: Moradi-Sepahvand and Tindemans (2024)
fillers.summary: Links day blocks in sequence and keeps extreme values with representative days and hours, in a model that plans lines, storage and wind farms together.

review_summary: Sorts the aggregation methods used in 130 publications by their assumptions, and lists open questions.

gap_q.q: No abstract in your twelve falls in the cell “{cell}”. Is that a research gap?
options: Yes: an empty cell is a gap
No: someone must have done it
Not yet: search that cell directly first

feedback.yes: Not yet. Twelve papers are a sample, and coding from abstracts can miss things. Search the cell itself before you claim it.
feedback.no: Too quick the other way: nobody knows until the cell is searched. Run the search, then read what it finds.
feedback.test: Right. An empty cell is a lead, not a gap. Turn it into a search string and log the result.

passes.label: First pass
passes.read: Title, abstract, introduction, section headings, conclusions; glance at the references you already know.
passes.out: The five Cs: category, context, correctness, contributions, clarity.

passes.label: Second pass
passes.read: Figures, tables and the argument; skip the proofs. Mark the references to read next.

passes.label: Third pass, optional
passes.time: 4–5 hours for a beginner, outside this studio's 4 hours
passes.read: Rebuild the work under the same assumptions, and challenge each one.
passes.out: What you would do differently, and what it would change.

headings: 1. Introduction (capacity expansion planning; time series aggregation; inter-period links and storage)
4. Simulation studies (overview; setup; validation; example; discussion)

five_cs.q: What kind of paper is it?
options: A new method, tested in simulations on a test system
A case study of one real country's plan
five_cs.worked: A methods paper: a new aggregation framework, tested in simulations on a six-region test system.

five_cs.q: Which papers does it build on?
five_cs.worked: Two from your matrix: Kotzur et al. (2018) for linked storage, and Teichgraeber, Küpper and Brandt (2021) for extreme periods taken from model results.

five_cs.q: Which assumptions will you check in pass two?
five_cs.worked: A test system based on the IEEE six-bus system; demand and wind only, no solar; operation with [[perfect-foresight|perfect foresight]].
Periods chosen after a first model run that keep chronology for storage and keep the extreme periods that drive capacity; models, data and code released.
Your judgement: note one thing you would ask the authors.

sheet.v: Can choosing periods after a first model run cut the error of capacity plans built from long weather series, in models with storage?
A six-region test grid: baseload, peaking and wind generation, transmission and storage, built from scratch.
Hourly demand and wind for European countries, 1980–2017, from a published [[reanalysis|reanalysis]]-based dataset.
Plan on representative days chosen from the input data; run operations over the full series; use those results to choose new periods, extreme and regular; plan again.
Three conventional schemes chosen from the input data alone and, on 3-year samples, the plan from the full series.
30 and 120 representative days; 40 resampled series; unserved energy checked over the full series.
Solar; operation without [[perfect-foresight|perfect foresight]] (named by the authors as an extension).

write_prompt: Draft your gap statement: what you searched (where, when, strings), what the matrix shows, what the direct search found, what a second pass on the closest paper showed, and the question that remains.

practice.task: Write two concept blocks for your own question; run five logged strings in OpenAlex, then adapt them to a second database's syntax (string as run, date, count).
Screen titles and abstracts down to about 30 candidates; note why you dropped the rest.
Find one review; snowball backward and forward from it; add what the searches missed.
Do a first pass on 12 papers (about 7 minutes each) and code them in a concept matrix with a written coding rule.
Search your empty cell directly and log the string, date and count.
Read the closest paper in a second pass, fill the extraction sheet, then write the gap statement.

practice_optional: Optional, beyond the 4 hours: a third pass on the closest paper (4–5 hours for a beginner).
databases_note: A string moves between databases only as far as their syntax allows. Log each search as you ran it there.

databases.name: OpenAlex
databases.syntax: AND, OR, NOT and quoted phrases: this page's strings run unchanged.
databases.log: String, field (titles and abstracts here), date, count.

databases.name: Semantic Scholar
databases.syntax: Quoted phrases, but no AND, OR or NOT on its search page: search one block's terms at a time.
databases.log: Each search as typed, date, how many results you screened.

databases.name: Crossref
databases.syntax: No AND, OR or exact phrases: it ranks works by how well their records match your words.
databases.log: The words as typed, date, how many results you screened.
databases.src: Crossref's answer on its community forum, March 2023, checked 8 November 2026

exemplars.task: Write the gap statement for the question above, from your search log, concept matrix and second-pass sheet.
weak: Representative periods are widely used, but

weak.note: No count, no database, no date: a reader cannot check it.
Undefined: linked between periods? Extremes chosen how?
A novelty claim the evidence cannot carry; a direct search finds at least three papers that do both.
Asserted, not shown: no matrix, no search of the cell.

good.note: Database, date and strings: anyone can repeat the search and see what has changed since.
Search and snowballing find different papers; together they found all twelve.

good.text: 12 papers coded from their abstracts by a written rule
good.note: The rubric's bar for positioning: at least 12 sources, coded with a stated rule.

good.text: no abstract reports both a storage link and extreme periods
good.note: Said as the coding allows: what the abstracts report, not what the papers lack.

good.text: a search of that cell returned 23 works; by their abstracts, at least three do both
good.note: The empty cell is tested, not assumed, and the gap as first stated does not survive.
